summary: This informational memo sets terminology for benchmarking eBGP convergence in the control plane of a single BGP device. It is meant to standardise how the methodology is described, with later documents covering other aspects.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4098 is a dictionary for measuring how quickly a BGP router reacts to a change in the routing information it is given. It defines words such as route instance, update train, route mixture, MRAI and device convergence, each with the units it should be reported in, so that a benchmark report from one vendor can be read against a report from another.

questions: how to measure bgp convergence speed
what is a bgp route instance
subtitle: The words a BGP convergence benchmark has to use, so that two results mean the same thing.

tldr.problem: Two people measuring how fast a BGP router converges could produce numbers that looked comparable and were not, because words like route, update, convergence and full table meant slightly different things to each of them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the vocabulary in five groups: the pieces of routing information, the tables a router keeps, the parts of a network, the sets of update messages, and the events and factors that decide how long convergence takes.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that defines no test. It is the first half of a two-document series, and the companion document holds the tests and methodology.

facts.label: Route instances to routes
facts.value: 4 to 10 times the number of routes

today: RFC 4098 is an Informational memo published in June 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the first of a two-document series on benchmarking BGP convergence; the companion document contains the tests and the methodology.

sections.title: Scope and Approach
sections.content:
RFC 4098 defines terminology for use in characterizing the convergence performance of BGP processes in routers or other devices that instantiate BGP functionality. It is the first part of a two-document series, of which the subsequent document will contain the associated tests and methodology. The terminology is applicable to both IPv4 and IPv6, and illustrative examples of each version are included where relevant. The document is primarily targeted at BGP-4 in IPv4 networks. IPv6 would require the use of MP-BGP, but this document does not address terminology or issues specific to those extensions of BGP-4, and terminology specific to the BGP extensions that support VPNs is out of scope.

Three observations underlie the approach. The principal objective is to derive methodologies that standardize conducting and reporting convergence-related measurements for BGP. It is necessary to remove ambiguity from many frequently used terms that arise in the context of these measurements. And because convergence characterization is a complex process, it is desirable to restrict the initial focus to specifying how to take basic control-plane measurements as a first step in characterizing BGP convergence. For path-vector protocols such as BGP, the initial focus is therefore on network and system control-plane activity consisting of the arrival, processing and propagation of routing information.

The memo says that for testing purposes all optional parameters SHOULD be turned off, and that all variable parameters SHOULD be at their default setting unless the test specifies otherwise. Later documents will explore the more intricate aspects of convergence measurement, such as the impact of the presence of Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4, policy processing, simultaneous traffic on the control and data paths within the device under test, and other realistic performance modifiers. Convergence of Interior Gateway Protocols will also be considered in separate documents.

Characterizing the convergence performance of a device has to take into account all the distinct stages and aspects of BGP functionality, which requires the relevant terms and metrics to be as specifically defined as possible. The definitions are classified into five groups: components and characteristics of routing information; routing data structures and route categories; descriptions of the constituent elements of a network or a router that is undergoing convergence; characterization of sets of update messages, types of route-change events, and events specific to BGP operation; and descriptions of factors that impact the performance of convergence processes.

Each term is presented in the same format as RFC 1812, with a definition, a discussion, the measurement units to report it in, any issues that could affect it, and related terms.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you can compare convergence times, you have to agree on what is being timed and what the inputs were. This memo fixes the words, and it also says that optional features should be switched off during a test so that the numbers describe the protocol rather than the extra features.

sections.title: The Pieces of Routing Information
sections.content:
The first group of definitions covers the parts of routing information.

A network prefix is a contiguous set of bits at the more significant end of the address that collectively designates the set of systems within a network, and host numbers select among those systems. This definition is taken directly from RFC 1812. In the CIDR context the network prefix is the network component of an IP address. In IPv4 the network component is known as the network part and the remainder as the host part; in IPv6 the network component is known as the subnet prefix and the remainder as the interface identifier.

The network prefix length is the number of bits, out of the total constituting the address field, that define the network prefix portion of the address. A common alternative to a bit-wise mask is slash notation, which binds the notion of prefix length in bits to an IP address: 141.184.128.0/17 indicates that the network component of that IPv4 address is 17 bits wide, and the same notation is used for IPv6, for example 2001:db8:719f::/48. When referring to groups of addresses, the prefix length is often used to describe them as an equivalence class, so one hundred /16 addresses refers to 100 addresses whose network prefix length is 16 bits. The measurement unit is bits.

A route is in general the n-tuple prefix, next hop and, optionally, other routing or non-routing protocol attributes. A route is not end-to-end, but is defined with respect to a specific next hop that should take packets on the next step toward their destination as defined by the prefix. A route is the basic unit of information about a target destination distilled from routing protocols. A BGP route is the n-tuple prefix, next hop, AS path and, optionally, other BGP attributes. BGP attributes such as next hop or AS path are the qualifying data that define the route.

The Network Level Reachability Information consists of one or more network prefixes with the same set of path attributes. Each prefix in the NLRI is combined with the common path attributes to form a BGP route, so the NLRI encapsulates a set of destinations to which packets can be routed along a common route described by the path attributes. A BGP UPDATE message contains an advertisement of a single NLRI field, possibly containing multiple prefixes, and multiple withdrawals of unfeasible routes. In every UPDATE a variable length sequence of path attributes is present, and each path attribute is a triple of attribute type, attribute length and attribute value.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the pieces a BGP message is made of: an address prefix, the number of bits of that prefix that are fixed, a next hop, and a list of attributes. One UPDATE message can carry many prefixes as long as they all have the same attributes, and it can also withdraw routes that have become unreachable.

sections.title: Routing Data Structures and Route Categories
sections.content:
The second group covers the tables a router keeps and the categories of route within them.

The Routing Information Base collectively consists of a set of logically, though not necessarily physically, distinct databases. The RIB contains all destination prefixes to which the router may forward, and one or more currently reachable next hop addresses for them. Routes included in this set potentially have been selected from several sources of information, including hardware status, interior routing protocols and exterior routing protocols. RFC 1812 contains a basic set of route selection criteria relevant in an all-source context, and many implementations impose additional criteria, a common one being the preference given to different routing information sources.

Adj-RIB-In and Adj-RIB-Out are views of routing information from the perspective of individual peer routers. The Adj-RIB-In contains information advertised to the device under test by a specific peer, and the Adj-RIB-Out contains the information the device under test will advertise to that peer. The Loc-RIB contains the set of best routes selected from the various Adj-RIBs, after applying local policies and the BGP route selection algorithm. The separation implied among the various RIBs is logical and does not necessarily follow that they are distinct and separate entities in any given implementation. Types of routes to consider include internal BGP, external BGP, interface, static and IGP routes.

Prefix filtering is a technique for eliminating routes from consideration as candidates for entry into a RIB by matching the network prefix in a BGP route against a list of network prefixes. A BGP route is eliminated if, for any filter prefix in the list, the route prefix length is equal to or longer than the filter prefix length and the most significant bits of the two prefixes match over the length of the filter prefix.

Routing policy is the ability to define conditions for accepting, rejecting and modifying routes received in advertisements. Policy is implemented using filters and associated policy actions such as prefix filtering, and many autonomous systems formulate and document their policies using the Routing Policy Specification Language and then automatically generate configurations for the BGP processes in their routers. The routing policy information base is the set of incoming and outgoing policies. Incoming policies are applied in phase 1 of the BGP selection process to the Adj-RIB-In routes, to set the metric for the phase 2 decision process; outgoing policies are applied in phase 3 to the Adj-RIB-Out routes, preceding route announcements to a specific peer. Policies have matching and action conditions, and the common information to match includes route prefixes, AS paths and communities. The action on a match may be to drop the update and not pass it to the Loc-RIB, or to modify the update in some way, such as changing local preference on input or MED on output, adding or deleting communities, or prepending the current AS in the AS path. The amount of policy processing will impact the convergence time and properties of the distributed BGP algorithm, and may vary from a simple policy that accepts all routes to a complex policy with a substantial fraction of the prefixes being filtered.

The Forwarding Information Base is the table containing the information necessary to forward IP datagrams, and at minimum contains the interface identifier and next hop information for each reachable destination network prefix. It is distinct from the routing table, which holds all routing information received from routing peers. It is a data plane construct used for the forwarding of each packet, and is generated from the RIB; for the purposes of this document the FIB is effectively the subset of the RIB used by the forwarding plane to make per-packet forwarding decisions. All the route computation and convergence occurs before entries are downloaded into a FIB.

The remaining terms in this section describe the processes and their relationships. A BGP instance is a process with a single Loc-RIB, and a test generator acting as multiple peers will typically run more than one instance while a router will typically run a single one. A BGP device is a system that has one or more BGP instances running on it, each responsible for executing the BGP state machine; it may be a traditional router, a route server, a BGP-aware traffic steering device, or a non-forwarding route reflector. A BGP session is a session between two BGP instances, and an active BGP session is one that is in the established state. A BGP peer is another BGP instance to which the device under test is in the established state, and a BGP neighbor is a device that can be configured as a BGP peer.

Two timers matter. The MinRouteAdvertisementInterval determines the minimum time between advertisements of routes to a particular destination from a single BGP device. The timer is applied on a pre-prefix basis, although it is set on a per-BGP device basis. Because a BGP instance may manage in excess of 100,000 routes, RFC 1771 allows a degree of optimization in order to limit the number of timers needed. The MRAI does not apply to routes received from BGP speakers in the same AS, nor to explicit withdrawals, and random jitter is recommended to avoid synchronization effects between the BGP instances in a network. The MinASOriginationInterval specifies the minimum interval between advertisements of locally originated routes from a BGP instance, with random jitter applied for the same reason.

Finally the memo distinguishes three kinds of route. An active route is a route for which there is a FIB entry corresponding to a RIB entry. A unique route is a prefix for which there is just one route instance across all Adj-RIBs-In, and a non-unique route is a prefix for which there is at least one other route in a set including more than one Adj-RIB-In. A route instance is one of several possible occurrences of a route for a particular prefix: when a router has multiple peers from which it accepts routes, routes to the same prefix may be received from several peers, and each route instance is associated with a specific peer. The BGP algorithm that arbitrates between the available candidate route instances may reject a specific route instance due to local policy. The number of route instances in the Adj-RIB-In bases will vary with the function performed by the router, and an inter-provider border router, located in the default-free zone, will likely receive more route instances than a provider edge router closer to the end users.
sections.plainLanguage: A BGP router keeps several views of what it knows: what each peer told it, what it will tell each peer, the best of all that, and the short list the packet forwarder actually uses. The memo names each one. It also names the two timers that decide how often a router is allowed to speak, and the distinction between a route that only one peer offered and one that several peers offered.

sections.title: The Routers and Tables Being Benchmarked
sections.content:
The third group describes the elements of a router or a network of routers. Many of these terms were originally described in previous standards or papers, and are included because of their pertinence to the discussion.

An individual router's routing table may not necessarily contain a default route, but not having a default route is not the same as having a full default-free table. A router that has a full set of routes as in a default-free table, but that also has a discard rule for a default route, would not be considered default free. In this section the references to number of routes are to routes installed in the Loc-RIB, which are therefore unique routes rather than route instances, and the total number of route instances may be 4 to 10 times the number of routes.

A default route can match any destination address. If a router does not have a more specific route for a particular packet's destination address, it forwards the packet to the next hop in the default route entry, provided the Forwarding Table contains one. The notation for a default route for IPv4 is 0.0.0.0/0 and for IPv6 it is 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0 or ::/0.

A default-free routing table has no default routes, and is typically seen in routers in the core or top tier of routers in the network. Core and top tier routers are not configured with a default route, and therefore forward every packet to a specific next hop based on the longest match between the destination IP address and the routes in the forwarding table. Default-free routing table size is commonly used as an indicator of the magnitude of reachable Internet address space, although such tables may also include routes internal to the router's AS. A full default-free table is the union of all sets of BGP routes taken from all the default-free BGP routing tables collectively announced by the complete set of autonomous systems making up the public Internet. Due to the dynamic nature of the Internet, the exact size and composition of this table may vary slightly depending on where and when it is observed. It is generally accepted that a full table does not contain the infrastructure routes or individual sub-aggregates of routes that are otherwise aggregated by the provider before announcement to other autonomous systems. The default-free zone is the part of the Internet backbone that does not have a default route. A full provider-internal table is a superset of the full routing table that contains infrastructure and non-aggregated routes, and experience has shown that it might contain 1.3 to 1.5 times the number of routes in the externally visible full table, so tables of that size are a real-world requirement for key internal provider routers.

The memo then names four classes of BGP-speaking router, which a given router may combine according to its logical location in the network. A provider edge router is a router at the edge of a provider's network that speaks eBGP to a BGP speaker in another AS. Traffic transiting it may be destined to or originate from non-adjacent autonomous systems, and in particular the MED values used there are not visible in those non-adjacent autonomous systems. It will always speak eBGP and may speak iBGP. A subscriber edge router is a router at the edge of the subscriber's network that speaks eBGP to its provider's ASes; it belongs to an end user organization that may be multihomed, and carries traffic only to and from that end user AS. It will always speak eBGP and may speak iBGP. An inter-provider border router is a BGP speaking router that maintains BGP sessions with other BGP speaking routers in other providers' ASes; traffic transiting it may be originated in or destined for another AS that has no direct connectivity with this provider's AS, and it will always speak eBGP and may speak iBGP. A core router is a provider router internal to the provider's network, speaking iBGP to that provider's edge routers, other intra-provider core routers, or the provider's inter-provider border routers; it will always speak iBGP and may speak eBGP.
sections.plainLanguage: A benchmark has to say what it measured against. The memo names the kinds of table a router can hold, from a small one with just a default route to the whole global table, and the four jobs a BGP router can be doing, because a router on the edge of a network and a router in the middle have very different amounts of work.

sections.title: Update Trains, Route Mixtures and Route Changes
sections.content:
The fourth group characterizes sets of update messages and the changes they carry. The packet train concept was originally introduced by Jain and Routhier and is here adapted to refer to a train of packets of interest in BGP performance testing. This is a formalization of the sort of test stimulus expected as input to a device under test running BGP: it could be a well characterized, ordered and timed set of hand-crafted BGP UPDATE packets, or it could just as well be a set of BGP UPDATE packets captured from a live router. The question of interest for this work is the identification of suitable update trains, modelled on or taken from live traces that reflect realistic sequences of UPDATEs and their contents.

Route packing is the number of route prefixes accommodated in a single routing protocol UPDATE message, either as updates, additions or modifications, or as withdrawals. In BGP a single UPDATE may contain two sets of multiple network prefixes: one set of additions and updates with identical attributes, the NLRI, and one set of unfeasible routes to be withdrawn. A route mixture is the demographics of a set of routes, and is the input data for the benchmark. The particular route mixture used as input must be selected to suit the question being asked of the benchmark: simple route mixtures might be suitable to test the performance limits of the BGP device, while using live data, or input that simulates live data, improves understanding of how the device will operate in a live network. The parameters identified as affecting the route mixture are path length distribution, attribute distribution, prefix length distribution, packet packing, and the probability density function of inter-arrival times of UPDATEs. Each is more complex than a single number.

An update train is a set of routing protocol UPDATE messages sent by a router to a BGP peer. The arrival pattern of UPDATEs can be influenced by many things, including TCP parameters, hold-down timers, upstream processing, a peer coming up, or multiple peers sending at the same time, and network conditions such as a local or remote peer flapping a link. Characterizing the profiles of real-world UPDATE trains is a matter for future research, and to generate realistic ones a formal mathematical scheme or a proven heuristic is needed to drive the selection of prefixes.

A random update train contains a route mixture randomized across NLRIs, updates and withdrawals, prefixes, and inter-arrival times of the UPDATEs, and possibly across other variables. This is intended to simulate the unpredictable asynchronous nature of the network, whereby UPDATE packets may have arbitrary contents and be delivered at random times. It is important that the data set be randomized sufficiently to avoid favouring one vendor's implementation over another's: the distribution of prefixes could be structured to favour the internal organization of the routes in a particular vendor's databases, and this is to be avoided. A route flap is a change of state, withdrawal, announcement or attribute change, for a route. Route flapping can be considered a special and pathological case of update trains, and a bench-marker SHOULD use a mixture of different route change events in testing.

The memo adopts a taxonomy of route change events proposed in RIPE-37 and by Labovitz and others, because these tests must tie in to phenomena that arise in actual networks. A route can be changed implicitly by replacing it with another route, or explicitly by withdrawal followed by the introduction of a new route; in either case the change may be an actual change, no change, or a duplicate. The four categories are AADiff, an implicit withdrawal of a route and replacement by a route different in some path attribute; AADup, an implicit withdrawal and replacement by a route identical in all path attributes; WADiff, an explicit withdrawal and replacement by a different route; and WADup, an explicit withdrawal and replacement by a route identical in all path attributes. The memo then extends the notation to describe the sequence of events from the update train's point of view: Tup for a route advertised to the device under test by test device x, Tdown for a route being withdrawn by device x, Tupinit for the initial announcement of a route to a unique prefix, and TWF for a route fail over after an explicit withdrawal. Each of these can involve a single route, a short packet train, or a full routing table, so the notation is extended: Tup(1,TDx) means device x sends one route, Tup(S,TDx) means device x sends a train of S routes, and Tup(DFT,TDx) means device x sends an approximation of a full default-free table. Finally, because the basic criterion for selecting a better route is the final tiebreaker defined in RFC 1771, the router ID, the memo uses descriptor events for routes selected by the BGP selection process: Tbest for the current best path, Tbetter for advertising a path better than Tbest, and Tworse for advertising a path worse than Tbest.
sections.plainLanguage: The input to a convergence test is a stream of BGP messages, and the memo gives that stream a vocabulary: how many routes fit in one message, what mix of routes the stream contains, and the train of messages itself. It also names the kinds of change a test can make to a route, from replacing one path with a slightly different one to withdrawing it and putting back the same one.

sections.title: Convergence, Reset Events and the Factors That Affect Them
sections.content:
A routing device is said to have converged at the point in time when the device under test has performed all actions in the control plane needed to react to changes in topology in the context of the test condition. For example, when considering BGP convergence, the convergence resulting from a change that alters the best route instance for a single prefix at a router would be deemed to have occurred when this route is advertised to its downstream peers. By contrast, OSPF convergence concludes when SPF calculations have been performed and the required link states are advertised onward. The convergence process can in general be subdivided into three distinct phases: convergence across the entire Internet, convergence within an autonomous system, and convergence with respect to a single device. Convergence with respect to a single device can be convergence with regard to the data forwarding processes, or convergence with regard to the routing processes, which is the focus of this document. The definition is intended, as far as is possible, to exclude any additional time needed to download and install the forwarding information base in the data plane.

The memo says it is of key importance to benchmark the performance of each phase of convergence separately before proceeding to a composite characterization of routing convergence, where implementation-specific dependencies are allowed to interact. Care also needs to be taken to ensure that the convergence time is not influenced by policy processing on downstream peers. The time resolution needed to measure device convergence depends to some extent on the types of the interfaces on the router: for modern routers with gigabit or faster interfaces, an individual UPDATE may be processed and re-advertised in very much less than a millisecond, so time measurements must be made to a resolution of hundreds to tens of microseconds or better. The measurement unit is a time period.

Two BGP operation events are defined. A hard reset is an event that triggers a complete re-initialization of the routing tables on one or more BGP sessions, resulting in exchange of a full routing table on one or more links to the router. A soft reset is performed on a per-neighbor basis; it does not clear the BGP session while re-establishing the peering relation and does not stop the flow of traffic. There are two methods of performing a soft reset: graceful restart, wherein the BGP device that has lost a peer continues to forward traffic for a period of time before tearing down the peer's routes, and soft refresh, wherein a BGP device can request a peer's Adj-RIB-Out.

The memo then lists the factors that affect the performance of the convergence process, though not a complete list, and says not all of them can be addressed in the baseline measurements. The general factors are conditions of testing external to the router. As the number of peers increases, the BGP route selection algorithm is increasingly exercised, and the phasing and frequency of updates from the various peers have an increasingly marked effect on convergence, depending on the quantity of updates generated by each additional peer; the number of peers also increases the processing workload for TCP and BGP keepalives. The number of routes per peer is an obvious stressor, and the number and relative proportion of multiple route instances and distinct routes being added or withdrawn by each peer will affect the process, as will the mix of overlapping route instances and IGP routes. Policy processing and reconfiguration matters in proportion to the number of routes and attributes being filtered and set as a fraction of the target route table size, from the minimal policy of receive all and send all to extensive policy where up to 100% of the total routes have applicable policy. Interactions with other protocols take the form of precedence, synchronization, duplication and the addition of timers and route selection criteria, and understanding BGP-4 convergence must include understanding the interactions with both the IGPs and the protocols associated with the physical media, such as Ethernet, SONET and DWDM. Flap damping is not mandatory, so enabling it and changing its parameters is a matter of routing policy; it requires the device to keep additional state, which can have a direct impact on the control plane through increased processing, and it may delay the arrival of real changes in a route. Churn refers to control-plane processor activity caused by announcements received and sent by the router, and does not include keepalives and TCP processing; it is caused by both normal and pathological events, and flapping routes and MED oscillation are pathological contributors to it.

The implementation-specific factors are conditions of testing internal to the device under test. The presence of actual forwarded traffic in the device may stress the control path if both the offered load and the control traffic, such as FIB updates and downloads as a consequence of flaps, are excessive, and adding data traffic presents a more accurate reflection of realistic operating scenarios than control traffic alone. The settings of delay and hold-down timers at the link level, as well as for BGP-4, can introduce or ameliorate delays, and as part of a test report all relevant timers MUST be reported if they use non-default values. Because all BGP traffic and interactions occur over TCP, all relevant parameters characterizing the TCP sessions MUST be provided, for example slow start, maximum window size, maximum segment size, or timers. Finally, authentication in BGP is currently done using the TCP MD5 Signature Option, and the processing of the MD5 hash, particularly in devices with a large number of BGP peers and a large amount of update traffic, can have an impact on the control plane of the device.

The memo's security considerations note that the document explicitly considers authentication as a performance-affecting feature, but does not consider the overall security of the routing system.
sections.plainLanguage: Convergence is reached when the router has done everything the routing process needs to do, not when the packets start flowing; the time to push the result into the forwarding table is deliberately left out. The last part of the memo lists everything that makes one router converge faster than another: how many peers it has, how many routes each holds, how much filtering it does, whether damping is on, and how much traffic is flowing through it at the same time.
